articles.title: PARALLEL VS. SERIAL
articles.summary: Serial processing is better for tasks that must be completed in a specific order and best performed by the CPU. Parallel processing is better for tasks that can be divided into many parts and done simultaneously and is best performed by a GPU. Many problems benefit from the fusion of both approaches, where the main problem is broken into many smaller independent problems solved in parallel. The solutions of the smaller problems can then be integrated serially to create the complete solution.

articles.summary: Organic marketing works best when founders define one specific buyer, study their language and communities, then design content packaging around behavior. Test hooks and formats, read retention signals, repurpose winning ideas by platform, and automate repetitive research and packaging.

articles.title: THE LEAD INVESTOR PROBLEM
articles.summary: A founder can fill a calendar with investor meetings and still have no round. "Interested," "keep us posted," and "we could participate" sound positive, but none means an investor will set the terms, anchor the valuation, do the deepest diligence, or give everyone else a deadline. A lead does those jobs. Keep likely leads separate from likely followers, then ask directly whether each fund would actually set the terms. Ten more meetings with followers still leave the lead column empty.

articles.title: PREVENTING CHURN IN SET-AND-FORGET PRODUCTS
articles.summary: Backups and monitoring can be working perfectly even when nobody logs in. One company with hundreds of thousands of customers searched its first 30 days of human activity for something that predicted who would still pay 12, 18, or 24 months later. It found nothing. The integration was doing the work, so the useful signals were whether data was still moving, volume was falling, or errors were rising. A cancellation may arrive months after the product stopped working, which means the real churn date happened much earlier.

articles.title: WE SPEND $45,000 ON DOING MORE WEIRD EVERY MONTH
articles.summary: PostHog sets aside $45,000 every month for marketing ideas that may fail. Anyone can pitch one in Slack, and a two- or three-person "Council of Weird" scores the cost, effort, and whether people actually want to make it. Some bets did almost nothing. Billboards got zero comments, Easter eggs were found by about three people, and a documentary got 2,000 views. Most startups can steal the setup for far less money by fixing what they are willing to lose each month and judging several experiments together.

articles.title: BUILDING A DIVERSIFIED STARTUP PORTFOLIO
articles.summary: Diversifying startup investments by sector, stage, and geography can mitigate risks associated with market volatility. Sector diversification helps balance industry-specific cycles, while stage diversification mixes potential high-reward early-stage investments with more stable later-stage companies. Geographic diversification protects against regional economic fluctuations, though it can be challenging to access international deals.
